title: Oxfordia Private Egress & Transit Gateway Readiness
summary: Initial network intake for a private Redwood deployment. Oxfordia requires no public egress, fixed outbound IPs for allowlisting, cross-account transit gateway in AWS, and region gating for EU-only data. Discussed PrivateLink vs VPC peering tradeoffs, DNS split-horizon, and KMS integration. Agreed on network workshop and security docs to be shared.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-21 16:00 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Tom Hargreaves (Oxfordia Head of Platform), Priya Rao (Oxfordia Security), Liam O'Neal (CTO), Sana Mirza (Network)

Summary: Rapid intake for private deployment networking and egress constraints. Customer is exploring Private (VPC) deployment with strict no-public-egress policy and needs predictable egress IPs for downstream SaaS allowlisting. They run multi-account AWS with a Transit Gateway and have EU data residency requirements.

Topics / Agenda:
- Current infra and transit topology
- Egress and NAT options (central NAT vs per-account NAT)
- Private endpoints vs VPC peering vs PrivateLink
- DNS & split-horizon considerations
- KMS/HSM and audit logging requirements
- Pilot plan and next steps

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick intros from our side, I'm Maya, AE, and Diego's our SE.
[00:08] Tom: Hi, Tom here. I'll start — I'm head of platform at Oxfordia.
[00:11] Priya: Priya, security team.
[00:13] Liam: Liam, CTO.
[00:14] Sana: Sana, network.
[00:16] Diego: Great, can you give a brief description of what you currently run and the trigger for going private?
[00:23] Tom: Sure. We run a multi-account AWS setup, Transit Gateway in use, a lot of internal services. We're piloting LLM features inside customer workflows so data residency and no public egress is a hard requirement. We're evaluating Redwood Private because we need the same API surface as hosted but with VPC-level isolation.
[00:38] Maya: Perfect. When you say no public egress, is that for model inference traffic as well or outbound to telemetry SaaS?
[00:45] Priya: Both. We cannot have raw inference payloads leaving the VPC to third-party endpoints. Also any logs need to be routed to our internal ELK or archived to S3 in EU with SSE-KMS.
[00:56] Diego: Got it. A couple of common patterns — we can do direct VPC peering to our private infra or we can expose PrivateLink endpoints. For multi-account, Transit Gateway usually simplifies routing. Does your platform prefer a centralized NAT egress or per-account NAT?
[01:12] Sana: We currently use a centralized NAT in the security account hooked to the TGW. That gives us a small number of egress IPs. But switching is possible if Redwood needs different topology.
[01:22] Maya: That's good because fixed egress IPs are usually what enterprises ask for — allowlisting for downstream services. Could you ballpark concurrent RPS or total TPS for inference calls? That helps sizing.
[01:33] Tom: At pilot maybe 50 TPS, production could be 400–800 TPS depending on model batch sizes. But initial pilot small.
[01:42] Diego: Okay that'll map to a modest set of pods — but the key is whether you need TLS interception or any outgoing proxy that terminates TLS.
[01:50] Priya: No TLS interception. End-to-end TLS is a must. KMS-managed keys on our side for S3, and we will want to wrap any exported logs with our KMS. Also audit logs per request — retention 1 year.
[02:03] Diego: Redwood Private supports customer KMS for storage encryption and we can ship audit logs to an S3 bucket over a private endpoint. There are two integration patterns: Redwood writes logs to our connector that pushes to your S3, or we have your S3 mounted via VPC endpoint. Which one do you prefer?
[02:19] Priya: Prefer push to our S3 over a VPC endpoint — but everything must stay on the private dataplane.
[02:25] Maya: We'll include a security pack explaining both flows.
[02:29] Liam: Region gating — we need inference processed only inside eu-west-1. Is that something you can enforce?
[02:36] Diego: Yes. Redwood Private can deploy in your target region. For our hosted fallback options, we can restrict routing so no requests leave the EU. With Dedicated or Private we can pin model instances in specific AZs/regions.
[02:48] Tom: Good. One risk: some downstream SaaS we use for analytics only accept allowlisting of IP ranges that are static. Can Redwood guarantee a small set of stable egress IPs?
[03:00] Maya: For Private in your VPC the egress IPs are the ones you control (the NAT or egress gateway). If you want Redwood-managed egress via our peering, we can provide ranges but they'd be from our side and may change with scale — not ideal.
[03:15] Priya: So we should probably host the egress in our account to keep the IP stable.
[03:19] Diego: That also simplifies audit and VPC flow logs. With the Transit Gateway you can route Redwood subnets to the central NAT. Also recommended: prefix-lists for quick updates.
[03:30] Sana: On the peering vs PrivateLink question, latency matters for us — sub 100ms for inference. PrivateLink introduces an NLB and some hairpinning. We've seen a minor hit but usually okay. Thoughts?
[03:44] Diego: PrivateLink can introduce a small additional hop. For latency-sensitive traffic we often recommend VPC peering or colocated subnets across a TGW. PrivateLink shines when you want to centralize service endpoints and avoid cross-account routing complexity. Since you have a TGW, peering routes across TGW are straightforward.
[03:59] Tom: Are there any limitations with split-horizon DNS? We run internal domains for service discovery and we'd want Redwood endpoints to resolve to internal IPs.
[04:08] Maya: We can support split-horizon via your internal DNS pointing to private IPs — we provide the internal IP ranges and you can create A records in your Route53 private hosted zone. There's some coordination for certs; mutual TLS isn't required but you can do mTLS if you need.
[04:23] Priya: Certificates — can Redwood support SNI and SANs for internal hostnames?
[04:27] Diego: Yes, we support SAN-based certs; we can either use Redwood-managed certs within the private net or you can bring your own if you want full control. We'll note the options in the docs.
[04:37] Liam: On KMS — we need HSM-backed keys (AWS CloudHSM) for wrapped keys. Does Redwood support KMIP or CloudHSM?
[04:46] Maya: We integrate with customer-managed KMS for object encryption. For HSM-level attestation we have an enterprise integration path we can discuss; may require an architecture call. We'll include the KMS integration guide in the security pack.
[04:59] Tom: One more on network: egress to third-party SaaS — some SaaS do allow only a handful of IPs and they require IPv4. We need a guarantee of IPv4 stable addresses.
[05:12] Diego: If you host the NAT in your account you control those IPv4 addresses and can guarantee them. If Redwood hosts egress we'd provide ranges but can't promise they never change.
[05:24] Sana: OK, we'll probably host NAT. Also curious about connectivity to on-prem. We have an on-prem DC that peering to AWS is through a VPN into the TGW — latency is ~40–60ms. Is that acceptable for your caches?
[05:36] Diego: Yes, that's within reasonable range for most LLM caching. For large KV cache round trips we prefer keeping that traffic inside the region, but initial pilot should be fine.
[05:46] Priya: Any special firewall rules needed for Redwood control plane? We want to limit management plane access to specific IPs.
[05:54] Maya: Control plane traffic is out-of-band; for Private deployments we can establish a private management channel or a peered control plane over our control connection. We'll provide the exact IPs and ports in the pack.
[06:05] Tom: How does rollout and fallback work? If a model goes unhealthy do you failover to a hosted variant? That would break our no-egress policy.
[06:13] Diego: Good catch. For Private we can configure automatic fallback policies: either failover within the same VPC to a compatible model, or disable external fallback. We'll default to no external fallback for strict customers.
[06:26] Liam: Pricing/commits — not detailed now, but pilot pricing and metrics are needed.
[06:31] Maya: We'll include a pilot quote and a ops SLO doc.
[06:35] Tom: OK, sounds good. Let's recap next steps.
[06:38] Maya: Recap: Diego will send network diagram template and sample TGW route table snippets. Priya will send egress whitelist and retention policy. I'll share security pack and pilot checklist. We'll schedule a 90-min network workshop next week to get into NAT, prefix-lists, route tables and certs.
[06:53] Priya: Quick Q — competitor BigCloud Endpoints said they do inline model inference inside our cluster. Any pros/cons?
[06:59] Diego: Inline can be lower latency but increases your operational burden — patching, driver dependencies, GPU scheduling. Redwood tries to offer that control via Private deployment without giving you full model ops burden; we still manage runtime with your network polices.
[07:14] Liam: Thanks all.
[07:16] Tom: Thanks, talk soon.

End of transcript.
